```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = FALSE, collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Use a database helper when you want to query with DBI or dbplyr. Each helper
returns a function such as `con`; call `con()` to get the signed-in user's
connection.

The snippets below replace parts of the [getting-started app](getting-started.html).
Create `client` outside `server()`, then create `auth` from that client
with `oauth_module_server()`. Put the `con` definition inside `server()`.

## Azure SQL

Install `odbc` and Microsoft ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server. Keep the
getting-started app's Microsoft client with `services = "sql"`.

```{r azure-sql}
con <- oauth_db_azure_sql(
  auth$connection,
  server = "example.database.windows.net",
  database = "Reporting"
)
```

The same helper can use SQL Managed Instance or Synapse SQL connection
settings. For SQL Server configured to accept Microsoft Entra tokens, use
`oauth_db_sql_server()` with its server and database. Your database
administrator must set up Entra access before the app can connect.

## Fabric SQL

Use this helper for a Warehouse, Lakehouse SQL analytics endpoint, or Fabric
SQL Database. Install `fabricQueryR` and `odbc`, plus Microsoft ODBC Driver 18.
Keep the Microsoft client with `services = "sql"`.

Copy the server and database from the intended item's SQL connection settings:

```{r fabric-sql}
con <- oauth_db_fabric_sql(
  auth$connection,
  server = "example.datawarehouse.fabric.microsoft.com",
  database = "Reporting"
)
```

For ADBC, pass `backend = "adbc"` after installing fabricQueryR's ADBC
dependencies and the MSSQL driver. Other connection options, such as `timeout`
and `read_only`, go directly to `fabricQueryR::fabric_sql_connect()`.

For OneLake files, DAX, or KQL, see [Platform APIs](platform-apis.html).

## Databricks SQL

Install `brickster`. Register a Databricks OAuth application and configure its
client ID, secret if issued, and redirect URI. Create this client outside
`server()`:

```{r databricks-client}
host <- "example.cloud.databricks.com"
client <- oauth_db_databricks_client(
  host = host,
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)
```

Inside `server()`, supply your SQL warehouse ID:

```{r databricks-dbi}
con <- oauth_db_databricks(
  auth$connection,
  host = host,
  warehouse_id = "warehouse-id",
  catalog = "main",
  schema = "reporting"
)
```

You can supply `http_path = "/sql/1.0/warehouses/warehouse-id"` instead of
`warehouse_id`. For Azure Databricks using Microsoft Entra authentication,
configure the Microsoft client with `services = "databricks_entra"` and set
`auth_mode = "entra"` on the connection helper.

## Snowflake

Install `odbc` and the Snowflake ODBC driver. Your account needs a Snowflake
OAuth integration and users with access to the requested role.

Create the sign-in client outside `server()`:

```{r snowflake-client}
client <- oauth_db_snowflake_client(
  server = "organization-account.snowflakecomputing.com",
  role = "REPORTING_READER",
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100"
)
```

Then create the connection inside `server()`:

```{r snowflake}
con <- oauth_db_snowflake(
  auth$connection,
  server = "organization-account.snowflakecomputing.com",
  role = "REPORTING_READER",
  warehouse = "REPORTING_WH",
  database = "ANALYTICS",
  schema = "PUBLIC"
)
```

You can omit `warehouse`, `database`, and `schema` to use the account's
defaults. Keep `role` consistent with the sign-in client.

For External OAuth through Entra, Okta, or another provider, keep that
provider's shinyOAuth configuration and supply the integration's `target`
and `required_scopes` to the connection helper. These settings depend on
your Snowflake integration.

## Amazon Redshift

Install `odbc` and the AWS Redshift ODBC 2.x driver with
`IdpTokenAuthPlugin` support. Your administrator must connect Redshift to
IAM Identity Center and configure its trusted issuer and user mapping.

For Microsoft Entra as that issuer, create this client outside `server()`.
Set the two Redshift environment variables to the resource and delegated
scope configured for your Entra registration:

```{r redshift-client}
client <- oauth_db_microsoft_client(
  tenant_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_TENANT_ID"),
  client_id = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_ID"),
  client_secret = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_CLIENT_SECRET"),
  redirect_uri = "http://localhost:8100",
  token_targets = list(redshift = list(
    resource = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_REDSHIFT_RESOURCE"),
    scopes = Sys.getenv("OAUTHDB_REDSHIFT_SCOPE")
  ))
)
```

Inside `server()`:

```{r redshift}
con <- oauth_db_redshift(
  auth$connection,
  server = "cluster.example.eu-west-1.redshift.amazonaws.com",
  database = "reporting",
  target = "redshift",
  token_type = "EXT_JWT"
)
```

`EXT_JWT` uses an external issuer's JWT access token. For an IAM Identity
Center access token, use `token_type = "ACCESS_TOKEN"` with the matching
shinyOAuth client. Other external identity providers can supply their own
client instead of the Microsoft example.

Set `driver` to the installed driver name or path if needed.
`CaFile` and `LoginTimeout` can be passed through to the driver.
The helper supplies the token, token type, and verified TLS settings, and
closes connections on account changes, sign-out, or session end.

## Azure PostgreSQL

Install `RPostgres` and use the Microsoft client with `services = "postgres"`.
Supply the database role provisioned for the user or their group:

```{r azure-postgres}
con <- oauth_db_azure_postgres(
  auth$connection,
  host = "example.postgres.database.azure.com",
  dbname = "reporting",
  user = "reporting-readers",
  sslrootcert = "path/to/root-ca.pem"
)
```

The server must accept Entra authentication. `sslrootcert` can be omitted if
libpq already has the correct CA bundle configured.

## Run a query

Once you've chosen a connection, use your usual database functions inside
a reactive expression:

```{r sql-query}
output$rows <- shiny::renderTable({
  connection <- con()
  DBI::dbGetQuery(connection, "SELECT * FROM products")
})
```

Call `con()` for each operation. This lets the helper check the current
sign-in and replace connections when needed. See each helper's help page for
driver options and [Authentication and sessions](authorization.html) for
permission settings, sign-out, and cached results.
